title: Logarithms: Meaning and Laws
summary: Revision of what a logarithm is, the laws of logarithms and the change of base formula.

p: A logarithm is the inverse of an exponent. If aˣ = y, then log_a y = x. Here a is the base (a > 0 and a ≠ 1), x is the logarithm (the power), and y is the number (y > 0). Read log_a y = x as 'log to base a of y is x'.
Examples: 2³ = 8 means log₂ 8 = 3. 10² = 100 means log₁₀ 100 = 2. 5² = 25 means log₅ 25 = 2. 3⁴ = 81 means log₃ 81 = 4. 2⁻³ = 1/8 means log₂ (1/8) = −3.
1. Product law: log_a (mn) = log_a m + log_a n. Example: log₂ (8 × 4) = 3 + 2 = 5, and 2⁵ = 32 = 8 × 4.
2. Quotient law: log_a (m/n) = log_a m − log_a n. Example: log₂ (16/4) = 4 − 2 = 2.
3. Power law: log_a (mⁿ) = n log_a m. Example: log₂ (8³) = 3 × 3 = 9, and 8³ = 512 = 2⁹.
4. log_a 1 = 0 for any base, because a⁰ = 1.
5. log_a a = 1, because a¹ = a.
6. Change of base: log_a m = log_b m ÷ log_b a. Example: log₂ 8 = log₁₀ 8 ÷ log₁₀ 2 = 0.9031 ÷ 0.3010 = 3.
Evaluate log₅ 125 + log₅ 25 − log₅ 5 = 3 + 2 − 1 = 4.
Evaluate 3 log₂ 8 − 2 log₂ 4 + log₂ 16 = 9 − 4 + 4 = 9.
Evaluate 2 log₂ 4 + 3 log₂ 2 − log₂ 8 = 4 + 3 − 3 = 4.
Express as a single logarithm: 2 log₁₀ x + log₁₀ y − 3 log₁₀ z = log₁₀ (x²y / z³).
The common logarithm has base 10 (the log button on a calculator). The natural logarithm has base e ≈ 2.718 (the ln button). They are related by ln x = 2.3026 × log₁₀ x.

title: Logarithmic and Exponential Equations and Calculations
summary: Solving equations that contain logarithms or unknown powers, checking for invalid answers, and using logarithms for calculations.

p: Change to exponential form. log₂ x = 5 gives x = 2⁵ = 32. log₁₀ x = 3 gives x = 1000. log₅ x = −2 gives x = 5⁻² = 1/25 = 0.04. log₃ (2x − 1) = 2 gives 2x − 1 = 9, so x = 5.

Example 1. log₂ x + log₂ (x − 3) = 2. Combine: log₂ [x(x − 3)] = 2, so x² − 3x = 4 and x² − 3x − 4 = 0. (x − 4)(x + 1) = 0, so x = 4 or x = −1. A logarithm needs a positive number, so x = −1 is rejected. Check x = 4: log₂ 4 + log₂ 1 = 2 + 0 = 2. Correct.
Example 2. log₃ (x + 2) − log₃ (x − 1) = 1. (x + 2)/(x − 1) = 3, so x + 2 = 3x − 3 and x = 2.5.
Example 3. 2 log₅ x = log₅ 9. x² = 9, so x = 3 (x = −3 is rejected).
Example 4. log₃ x + log₃ (x + 6) = 3. x(x + 6) = 27, x² + 6x − 27 = 0, (x + 9)(x − 3) = 0, so x = 3.
Example 6. log₂ x + log₂ (x − 7) = 3. x(x − 7) = 8, x² − 7x − 8 = 0, (x − 8)(x + 1) = 0, so x = 8.
If the bases can be matched, compare the powers: 3^(2x + 1) = 27 = 3³, so 2x + 1 = 3 and x = 1. 3^(x + 2) = 81 = 3⁴, so x = 2.
If not, take logarithms of both sides: 2ˣ = 10. x log 2 = 1, so x = 1 ÷ 0.3010 = 3.32. 5ˣ = 20: x = log 20 ÷ log 5 = 1.3010 ÷ 0.6990 = 1.86.

A population grows by P = P₀ × 2^(t/10), where t is in years. How long does 50 000 take to reach 200 000? 200 000 = 50 000 × 2^(t/10), so 2^(t/10) = 4 = 2². t/10 = 2, so t = 20 years. (By logarithms: (t/10) log 2 = log 4 = 2 log 2, so t/10 = 2.)
Use log to turn multiplication into addition and division into subtraction. 45.6 × 78.2: log 45.6 = 1.6590 and log 78.2 = 1.8932. Sum = 3.5522. Antilog = 3 566. Check: 45.6 × 78.2 = 3 565.9.
Always check your answer with a calculator.
2 log₅ x − log₅ (x − 4) = log₅ 4 gives x²/(x − 4) = 4, so x² − 4x + 16 = 0. Its discriminant is 16 − 64 = −48, which is negative, so there is no real solution.

title: Logic: Statements and Connectives
summary: What a statement is, and the connectives not, and, or, with their truth tables.

p: Logic is the science of correct reasoning. A statement (proposition) is a sentence that is either true or false, but not both. 'Lagos is in Nigeria' is true. '5 + 3 = 7' is false. 'Go to school!' is a command and 'What is your name?' is a question: neither is a statement. 'x + 5 = 10' is not a statement until x is given a value.
A simple statement has one idea (p: It is raining). A compound statement joins simple statements with connectives (It is raining and I am hungry).
The negation of p is written ~p or ¬p. It is true when p is false and false when p is true. If p is 'It is raining', ~p is 'It is not raining'.
p ∧ q is true only when both p and q are true.
p ∨ q is true when at least one of p and q is true (the inclusive or).
For two statements there are 4 rows (2²). For three there are 8 rows (2³). Work in steps, one column for each part.
Example: (p ∨ q) ∧ ~p. For p = T, q = T: (T) ∧ F = F. For T, F: T ∧ F = F. For F, T: T ∧ T = T. For F, F: F ∧ T = F. So the statement is true only when p is false and q is true.

title: Logic: Conditional and Biconditional Statements
summary: The conditional p → q and biconditional p ↔ q, and the converse, inverse and contrapositive of a conditional.

p: p → q reads 'if p, then q'. p is the hypothesis and q is the conclusion. Example: If it rains (p), then the ground is wet (q). The conditional is false only when the hypothesis is true and the conclusion is false. If the hypothesis is false the conditional is true (vacuous truth): a false hypothesis tells us nothing about the conclusion.
p ↔ q is true when p and q have the same truth value. Example: A number is divisible by 2 if and only if it is even.

For p → q: the converse is q → p (If the ground is wet, then it rained). The inverse is ~p → ~q (If it does not rain, the ground is not wet). The contrapositive is ~q → ~p (If the ground is not wet, then it did not rain).

A conditional and its contrapositive are logically equivalent (they always have the same truth value). The converse and inverse are equivalent to each other, but not to the original. In the example, the ground can be wet from a burst pipe, so the converse can be false even when the original is true.

sections.h: Show that p → q is equivalent to ~q → ~p
p: Row T, T: p → q is T; ~q → ~p is F → F = T. Row T, F: p → q is F; ~q → ~p is T → F = F. Row F, T: p → q is T; ~q → ~p is F → T = T. Row F, F: p → q is T; ~q → ~p is T → T = T. The two columns are identical (T, F, T, T), so they are equivalent.
(p → q) ∧ (q → p) has the same truth table as p ↔ q. The statement (p ∧ q) → r is false only when p and q are true and r is false.

title: Logic: Equivalence, Tautology and Valid Arguments
summary: Logical equivalence and De Morgan's laws, tautologies and contradictions, and testing whether an argument is valid.

p: Two statements are logically equivalent (≡) if their truth tables are identical.
De Morgan's laws: ~(p ∧ q) ≡ ~p ∨ ~q and ~(p ∨ q) ≡ ~p ∧ ~q.
Check the first: for T, T: ~(T) = F and F ∨ F = F. For T, F: ~(F) = T and F ∨ T = T. For F, T: T and T ∨ F = T. For F, F: T and T ∨ T = T. The columns match.
Other equivalences: p ∧ T ≡ p, p ∨ F ≡ p, p ∧ p ≡ p, p ∨ p ≡ p.
A tautology is always true: p ∨ ~p. A contradiction is always false: p ∧ ~p. A contingency can be true or false: p ∧ q.
An argument has premises (statements assumed true) and a conclusion. It is valid if the conclusion must be true whenever all the premises are true.
Valid: p → q, p, therefore q (modus ponens). In the only row where both premises are true (p = T, q = T), q is also true.
Valid: p → q, ~q, therefore ~p (modus tollens).
Invalid: p → q, q, therefore p (affirming the consequent). Take p = F and q = T: both premises are true but the conclusion p is false.

Premise 1: If a student studies, he passes. Premise 2: John studied. Conclusion: John passed. This is valid. But Premise 2: John passed; conclusion: John studied is invalid, because he may have passed in some other way.

title: Surds: Simplifying and Rationalising
summary: Simplifying surds, adding and multiplying them, and rationalising denominators.

p: A surd is an irrational root that cannot be written exactly as a fraction, such as √2, √3 and √5. We keep them in surd form for exact answers.
Remove the surd from the bottom. 1/√3 = √3/3. 2/√5 = 2√5/5.

With a binomial denominator multiply top and bottom by the conjugate (change the sign between the terms). 1/(1 + √2) = (1 − √2) / ((1 + √2)(1 − √2)) = (1 − √2) / (1 − 2) = √2 − 1. 3/(√5 − √2) = 3(√5 + √2) / (5 − 2) = √5 + √2.

title: Exact Trigonometric Values for 30°, 45° and 60°
summary: The exact values of sine, cosine and tangent of 30°, 45° and 60°, the CAST rule and worked examples with surds.

p: Use a right-angled isosceles triangle (sides 1, 1, √2) for 45° and half of an equilateral triangle (sides 1, 2, √3) for 30° and 60°.

In the four quadrants (0° to 360°): All ratios are positive in the first quadrant (0° to 90°). Sine only is positive in the second (90° to 180°). Tangent only is positive in the third (180° to 270°). Cosine only is positive in the fourth (270° to 360°). 'All Students Take Calculus' helps you remember.
sin²45° + cos²45° = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1 (so sin²θ + cos²θ = 1).

If sin θ = √3/2 and θ is acute: cos²θ = 1 − 3/4 = 1/4, so cos θ = 1/2, and tan θ = √3. So θ = 60°. Solve 2 cos x = √3 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 90°: cos x = √3/2, so x = 30°. If tan θ = √3 (acute), θ = 60°, sin θ = √3/2 and cos θ = 1/2.
An exercise asks to prove (sin 60° − sin 30°) / (cos 30° − cos 60°) = √3. Numerator = √3/2 − 1/2 = (√3 − 1)/2. Denominator = √3/2 − 1/2 = (√3 − 1)/2. They are equal, so the value is 1, not √3.

title: Graphs of Sine and Cosine and Solving Trigonometric Equations
summary: The shapes and properties of y = sin x and y = cos x for 0° to 360°, and solving simple trigonometric equations from the graph and by calculation.

p: Both graphs are smooth waves. Period: 360° (the pattern repeats every 360°). Amplitude: 1 (the greatest height). Range: −1 ≤ y ≤ 1.

y = sin x starts at 0, rises to 1 at 90°, falls to 0 at 180°, to −1 at 270° and returns to 0 at 360°. y = cos x starts at 1, falls to 0 at 90°, to −1 at 180°, rises to 0 at 270° and returns to 1 at 360°. The cosine graph is the sine graph shifted 90° to the left: cos x = sin (x + 90°).
The two graphs meet where sin x = cos x, at x = 45° and x = 225°.
